title: Envelo
description: Title slide: product one-liner, live on Arc Testnet, mainnet next.
speakerNotes: Open with the one-liner: invoices are sealed inside the sender's browser so nobody in the middle can read them, proof of the paperwork lives on Arc, and payment settles in USDC. Say plainly that the product runs today on Arc Testnet and that Arc mainnet launched on 17 September 2026; the mainnet plan comes at the end of the deck. Spend twenty seconds here, then move.

title: Invoices in the open
description: The two failures of email-and-PDF billing: leaked private data and unverifiable payment records.
speakerNotes: Billing today runs on emailed PDFs and shared drive links, and two things break: private details like rates and client names are readable by everyone who handles the email, and 'paid' is just a claim - a screenshot the other side cannot check, while an edited invoice looks identical to the original. Land the bottom line exactly as written: freelancers over-share, clients cannot prove, auditors cannot trust. No blockchain words are needed yet - this is a paperwork problem everyone in the room has had.

title: The sealed envelope
description: Envelope, wax stamp, one currency: the product explained in paper-mail terms.
speakerNotes: Walk the three parts left to right in paper-mail terms. The envelope: the invoice body is encrypted in the browser before anything is uploaded, so the server stores a sealed envelope it cannot open plus the metadata it needs to run (amount, due date, who the parties are), which the privacy page lists. The wax stamp: a fingerprint of the document is recorded on Arc, so anyone can check the document is untouched without seeing what is inside. The payment: one plain test-USDC transfer whose receipt stays pinned to the invoice - and the fact to land is that even we, the operators, cannot read the line items in our users' invoices.

title: Seal, anchor, pay, grant
description: The four-step flow across the three demo accounts.
speakerNotes: Introduce the three people once - Riya bills, Arjun pays, Meera audits - then read the four moves in order. Riya's browser seals the invoice; its fingerprint is anchored on Arc Testnet; Arjun pays in test USDC and the paid mark flips on the chain right next to that fingerprint; Meera gets a temporary key, and revoking it stops her next open - though nothing can take back what she already read. Tell the room these same four moves are exactly what the live demo will show in three slides.

title: What touches the chain
description: Data minimalism: browser, server, and Arc each hold only what they need.
speakerNotes: This is the privacy slide: each layer keeps only what it needs - the invoice is readable only in the browser, the server holds sealed envelopes and wrapped keys, and the chain holds the wax stamp and the payment record. Land the closing line: no names, no amounts, no addresses in the wax stamp - verify without revealing. If a judge notes that paying shows an amount and wallet addresses on the explorer, agree cheerfully: that public receipt is the point - the document and the people behind the wallets stay private. If someone asks why use a chain at all, the answer is that proof of the paperwork should not depend on trusting our server.

title: Why Arc
description: USDC as native gas, one-currency payments, and the network panel: Envelo today on testnet, next on mainnet.
speakerNotes: Three reasons Arc: gas is USDC so invoice, fee and balance share one unit; the client needs no second token; finality is under a second so the paid flag flips while both parties watch. The panel on the right is honest about where Envelo is: today on Arc Testnet (chain 5042002, test USDC), next on Arc mainnet (chain 5042, real USDC), which launched on 17 September 2026.

title: The live demo
description: Account-by-account walkthrough of the running app, plus the verify tool.
speakerNotes: Switch to the running app and walk the loop signing in as each demo account - mention these are real email sign-ups, not built-in roles, so anyone in the room could make their own. As Riya, create an invoice and point out the Sealed badge, then the explorer link once the anchor lands on Arc. As Arjun, open the same invoice, press Pay, and click the transaction hash so the room sees the real record on testnet.arcscan.app. As Meera, open it through the time-limited grant, revoke it and show the app now refuses to open it for her - then finish with Verify (available to the sender, the client, or a grantee), which recomputes the fingerprint in the browser and checks it against both the database and the chain.

title: Known limits
description: Testnet scope, custodial demo wallets, revoke honesty, the v3 contract's trust in the payer, and the no-mocked-receipts rule.
speakerNotes: Read the limits plainly - being upfront here earns trust rather than losing it. Everything runs on test USDC with no real-world value; the demo wallets are held server-side so nobody needs a browser extension, which the app discloses and which would never be acceptable for real funds; a revoked share only blocks the next open, because nothing can take back what was already read; the v3 registry flips "paid" on any positive transfer and the server trusts that flag, which is fine for a demo and not for money, so v4 binds payee and amount before mainnet; and one visit to Circle's faucet funds each demo wallet. If wallets come up, add the undersold part: sign-in is real email, envelope keys have passphrase-locked backups plus a change-key flow, and payouts can already go to an address a user brings - typed in, not ownership-proven. Close on the promise: the app never fakes a receipt - when the chain is not ready, it says so; private by default, verifiable when it matters.

title: What is live today
description: Six shipped capabilities, the honest stage label, and the testnet registry address.
speakerNotes: This is the traction slide, and it is deliberately honest: the product is public, works end to end on web and mobile, and is pre-revenue. Walk the six cards quickly: live web app since 31 August 2026, mobile app (push is built and turns on with the store build), the full seal-anchor-pay-grant-verify loop on the real chain, the v3 registry contract (two calls: anchor, then pay), key backup and lost-key reset, and an end-to-end suite that runs against Arc Testnet. Close on the registry address: anyone in the room can open it on the explorer right now.

title: The road to mainnet
description: Three-phase mainnet plan: anchoring, non-custodial payments, hardening; Envelo never holds customer money.
speakerNotes: Arc mainnet launched today, 17 September 2026. Phase 1: deploy registry v4 on chain 5042, which binds each payment to the payee and amount the sender committed to, and anchor fingerprints, paid by our operator wallet at about a tenth of a cent each; no customer funds move. Phase 2: clients pay from a wallet they control, Circle Wallets or an external wallet, and USDC lands directly with the sender, so Envelo is never a custodian. Phase 3: KMS-held operator key, audit log, CCTP and Gateway funding, and Arc's selective-disclosure privacy for the amount when it ships. The same codebase serves both chains; testnet stays the free sandbox.

title: Milestones and the ask
description: Three dated milestones with on-chain proof, plus the funding ask and use of funds.
speakerNotes: Each milestone has a public trace on Arc: the mainnet registry address in Q4 2026, the first invoice paid on mainnet from a client-owned wallet in Q1 2027, and ten businesses invoicing on mainnet in Q2 2027 with the CCTP and Gateway funding path live. State the ask and the runway, then the split: most of the money is engineering for these three milestones, a security review before mainnet payments, and pilots plus operations. Fill the bracketed numbers before presenting.

title: Team

speakerNotes: Introduce yourself: what you have built before and why invoicing. Everything in this deck was built on Arc since August 2026: the contract, the web app, the mobile app, and the test suite that runs against the chain. Finish with the ask to try the live app at envelo.online and the contact details. Replace the bracketed placeholders before sending.
